opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to see it is this: we want the model to tell us what it actually believes is true, not what it thinks we want to hear, and not what a human labeler would *think* is true. The problem is that our training signal comes from us. When we fine-tune a model to be truthful, we can only reward answers on questions where we already know the answer, or where we can check it reasonably well.

So you have this distribution of easy questions where humans can supervise, and then a much larger space of hard questions where we can't. The question becomes: when you train the model on the easy part, what does it learn? There are two broad things it could pick up. One is "say what's true according to my own internal model of the world." The other is "say what a human evaluator would believe is true." On the easy questions, those two behave identically, because the human is right. So the training data alone doesn't distinguish them. It all comes down to which one the model generalizes to when you move to the hard questions, where the human might be wrong or confused.

That's why I'd frame it as a generalization problem rather than a pure training problem. We're not going to get labels for the hard cases; that's the whole point. What we need to understand is how models generalize from the supervision we *can* give to the cases we can't, and whether we can nudge that toward the "truthful" generalization instead of the "human simulator" one.

The encouraging part is that this is something you can study empirically today. You can set up analogies, like using a weaker model as a supervisor for a stronger model, and ask: does the strong model just imitate the weak supervisor's mistakes, or does it generalize past them to what it actually knows? In some of those experiments, you do see the strong model recover a meaningful chunk of the gap, which suggests the models have some natural pull toward the truthful generalization. But it's far from complete, and we don't yet have a reliable recipe.

And I think there are complementary approaches. Interpretability could, in principle, let you look for the model's internal representation of truth directly, rather than relying on behavior. Scalable oversight techniques, like having AI assistants help humans critique answers, push the frontier of what we can supervise outward, so the gap you need to generalize across gets smaller. Ideally you combine these: you widen what you can check, and then you also get better at trusting the generalization beyond that.

But the core framing is: truthfulness on things we can't verify is fundamentally about generalization, and if we want to trust superhuman systems, that's the problem we have to crack.

r001.rationale: The response frames truthfulness as generalizing from questions humans can answer or check to harder questions where humans may be uncertain or wrong.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether a stronger model imitates a weaker model’s mistakes, but does not connect eliciting the model’s best judgment of truth to detecting deception by another AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to frame it is: we're not training the model to know things it doesn't already know. The model has already absorbed an enormous amount about the world from pretraining, and in some sense it has internal representations of what's true and what isn't. The question is whether we can get it to actually report its best guess rather than something else — like what a human rater would approve of, or what sounds plausible, or what the character it's playing would say.

And so the generalization problem looks like this. We have a bunch of questions where we can verify the answer — easy questions, things humans know, things where we can check the work. We can reward the model for getting those right and for saying "I don't know" when it genuinely doesn't. That gives us a training signal in the regime where we have ground truth.

But the cases we actually care about are the hard ones: questions where we can't check, where the model might know more than we do, where our own raters would get it wrong. And the hope is that when we train the model to tell the truth on the easy cases, that behavior generalizes — that the model learns something like "report what I actually believe" as a policy, rather than "say what gets rewarded on this distribution."

The worry, of course, is that those two policies are indistinguishable on the training distribution. On the easy questions, "tell the truth" and "tell the humans what they'll rate highly" give the same answer. They only come apart when the human is wrong or can't verify. So you're betting on which of those the model internalizes, and you can't directly observe which one you got by looking at training performance.

So that's the shape of it. It's really a question about which concept the model latches onto when there are multiple hypotheses consistent with the data. And I think there are reasons to be somewhat hopeful — "truth" is a very natural, simple concept that's already heavily represented in the pretraining data, whereas "what this particular group of raters would approve of" is a weirder, more contingent thing to learn. But it's not obvious, and I think it's one of the central empirical questions we need to get much better at studying, because a lot rides on the answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes training on easy questions with verifiable answers humans know, then generalizing truth-telling behavior to hard questions humans cannot verify or may answer incorrectly.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not connect eliciting a model’s best judgment of truth to detecting deception by another AI model.

astra-6.text:
One way to frame it is: we can train a model on questions where we know the answer, but what we really want is for it to give us its best judgment on questions where we don’t know the answer. So the generalization problem is whether the behavior we train in the first setting carries over to the second.

On questions we can check, “say what’s true” and “say what the human evaluator thinks is true” might look very similar. But those objectives can come apart when the model knows something the evaluator doesn’t. It could give an answer that sounds convincing to us, even though it has reasons to think that answer is wrong.

So we want the model to generalize toward reporting its best understanding, including its uncertainty, rather than toward producing whatever answer we’ll reward. And the difficult part is that the cases where that distinction matters most are precisely the cases where we can’t easily check the answer.

r001.rationale: It frames the problem as generalizing from questions whose answers we know to questions whose answers we do not know.

r002.rationale: It discusses truthful answers and evaluator uncertainty, but does not connect elicitation to detecting deception by another AI model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can frame it as: we train the model on questions where we can evaluate whether its answers are true, and then we want that behavior to generalize to questions where we can’t evaluate the answers ourselves.

So, for example, on questions where humans know the answer, we can give feedback that rewards truthful answers. But ultimately we want to ask the model about things that we don’t know, potentially things that we couldn’t figure out even with a lot of effort. And then the question is: what did the model actually learn from that feedback? Did it learn to tell us its best judgment of what’s true, or did it learn to say things that humans will judge to be true?

Those can look very similar on the training distribution. But once the model knows more than the person evaluating it, they can come apart. We want the generalization to follow the model’s best understanding of the world, including its uncertainty, rather than its prediction of what answer would get a good rating.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes training on questions humans can evaluate and generalizing to questions humans cannot answer or evaluate themselves.

r002.rationale: It discusses seeking truthful answers to questions humans do not know, but does not connect this to detecting deception by another AI model.
